analysis.one_liner: Caps the total cost of consumer credit, including all fees, at 36% a year.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap consumer loan interest and fees at 36% nationwide was introduced by Sen. Durbin with 2 cosponsors and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which has taken no action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to make it illegal for any lender to charge a consumer more than 36% a year in interest and fees combined, on any type of credit. It counts everything toward that cap: interest, late fees, overdraft fees, cash advance fees, credit insurance, and fees on earned-wage advance apps. Loans that break the cap would be unenforceable, lenders would have to return all charges, violations could carry prison time and heavy fines, and state attorneys general could sue. The bill sits in the Senate Banking Committee with no scheduled action and only two cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who use high-cost credit: payday borrowers, car title borrowers, people hit with overdraft fees, and borrowers on subprime credit cards. The bill's own findings say these consumers pay roughly 400% annual interest on payday loans, 300% on car title loans, and about 17,000% effective annual rates on overdraft loans, with spending of about $12 billion on overdraft, $8.6 billion on payday, and $3.8 billion on car title loans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers using payday, title, and overdraft loans

how_it_helps.text: No creditor could extend consumer credit at a combined fee-and-interest rate above 36%, applied nationwide to all lenders regardless of state law or preemption loopholes.

The cap counts all charges connected to the loan, including interest, annual and membership fees, cash advance fees, late fees, insufficient funds fees, overdraft and over-limit fees, credit insurance, add-on products, and earned-wage advance fees, so lenders cannot evade the cap with fee games.

Loans made above the cap would be void and unenforceable, the lender would have to return all principal, interest, and fees, and violations could bring one year in prison plus a fine of up to triple the accrued debt or $50,000, whichever is greater.
State attorneys general could enforce the cap in federal court and seek injunctions, and states remain free to keep stronger protections.
The bill's findings cite the existing 36% cap for military families, enacted in 2006, as evidence that a cap curbed payday, car title, and tax refund lending around military bases.

The Bureau may allow small tolerances, such as modest application fees and limited late fees, only for loans paid in at least 3 installments over at least 90 days of $300 or more, keeping the door open to affordable small-dollar installment credit.

analysis.who_pays: High-cost lenders lose their current revenue stream: payday and car title lenders, banks that charge overdraft fees, online installment lenders, and subprime credit card issuers. Some borrowers who rely on expensive emergency credit might lose access to it if lenders stop offering it rather than lend at 36%, unless banks and credit unions step in with small-dollar installment loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday, title, overdraft, and subprime lenders

drawbacks.text: A 36% all-in cap would make many small-dollar and short-term loans unprofitable to offer. Borrowers with poor credit who use payday or title loans for emergencies could be cut off from credit entirely if affordable installment alternatives do not appear, a risk the bill itself acknowledges by urging that low-fee installment alternatives be encouraged.

Because the cap counts fees, it effectively ends most overdraft lending and fee revenue, which some low-balance checking account customers use to cover shortfalls; they would lose that cushion unless their bank offers a cheaper substitute.
Lenders who do offer credit near the cap would face stiff penalties, including voided loans and criminal exposure, which could make them overly cautious and shrink legitimate subprime lending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions who currently pay triple-digit effective rates, the benefit is large and concrete: a hard, loophole-proof 36% ceiling with real enforcement, modeled on the cap that already protects military families. The honest cost is that some borrowers who today rely on high-cost loans may lose that credit and face worse options, such as missed bills or unregulated lenders, unless mainstream lenders fill the gap with small-dollar installment products. The bill tries to manage that risk with tolerances for longer-term installment loans, but whether alternatives scale up is the open question.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on September 11, 2025, joined by Sens. Blumenthal and Whitehouse.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; the record shows no further action since.
Only two senators have signed on as cosponsors, both Democrats.

The bill lays out its case in findings: consumers pay roughly $12 billion on high-cost overdraft loans, $8.6 billion on payday loans, and $3.8 billion on car title loans, at average rates of about 400% for payday and 17,000% for overdraft.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: high-cost lenders continue to charge current rates, and the consumers paying them keep paying. The bill's fate depends on whether the Senate Banking Committee ever takes it up, and with two cosponsors and a committee not led by its party, no path to a vote is visible.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set a nationwide 36% all-in cap on consumer credit costs.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action since; no markup or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats are attached to the bill (the sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors), and Republicans hold the majority on the Banking Committee where the bill sits untouched.

industries.note: Their business model is built on rates averaging around 400% for payday and 300% for car title loans, which the cap outlaws; their gain is the public's cost. The bill's findings estimate consumers pay $8.6 billion on payday and $3.8 billion on car title loans.

The cap counts overdraft fees, which the bill's findings put at roughly $12 billion a year and an effective 17,000% annual rate for high-cost overdraft loans; banks would have to replace this with affordable small-dollar lending or lose the revenue.

industries.industry: Online installment and earned-wage advance lenders
industries.note: Triple-digit-rate online installment loans and fees on earned-wage advances are both swept into the 36% cap, removing their current pricing freedom.
Most credit cards already price under 36%, but subprime cards with high rates plus late and over-limit fees could breach the cap, shrinking that segment while leaving prime card lending untouched.

The cap could push emergency borrowers toward them, but only if their small-dollar installment products clear the 36% all-in test; the bill allows limited fee tolerances for loans of $300 or more paid over 90 days or more to keep that door open.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to the Senate Banking Committee and nothing has moved. A consumer credit cap with two cosponsors facing a committee run by the other party is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote this Congress; the realistic path is that it dies in committee unless a broader lending or overdraft debate forces it forward.
